```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(nlmixr2lib)
library(PKNCA)
library(rxode2)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
rxode2::rxSetSeed(20160101)
```

# Model and source

* Citation: `r readModelDb("Song_2016_olmesartan_QTcF")()$reference`
* Article: <https://doi.org/10.1002/jcph.572>
* Companion study report (design, demographics, NCA): Mendell J, Matsushima N,
  O'Reilly TE, Lee J. A thorough QTc study demonstrates that olmesartan
  medoxomil does not prolong the QTc interval. J Clin Pharmacol.
  2016;56(4):484-491. <https://doi.org/10.1002/jcph.610>

Song et al. (2016) analysed the thorough QTc study of olmesartan medoxomil, an
angiotensin II receptor blocker, in healthy adults. Each subject received single
oral doses of olmesartan medoxomil 40 mg (highest approved dose) and 160 mg
(supratherapeutic), placebo and moxifloxacin 400 mg in a four-period crossover.
The ECG endpoints were placebo-adjusted and baseline-adjusted ("double delta").
Fridericia's correction (QTcF) and a population correction (QTcP) both left some
heart-rate dependence at high heart rates. The authors therefore put the
baseline-adjusted, placebo-adjusted RR interval (DeltaDeltaRR) into the model as
a regressor beside the olmesartan concentration. They fitted the same linear
mixed-effects model to three endpoints. The package carries one file for each:

| Model file | Endpoint | Output | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| `Song_2016_olmesartan_QTc` | DeltaDeltaQT, no formula correction (the paper's "DeltaDeltaQTc") | `QTc` | Table 2, "QTc" columns |
| `Song_2016_olmesartan_QTcF` | DeltaDeltaQTcF, QTcF = QT / RR^0.33 | `QTcF` | Table 2, "QTcF" columns |
| `Song_2016_olmesartan_QTcP` | DeltaDeltaQTcP, QTcP = QT / RR^(1/3.265) | `QTcP` | Table 2, "QTcP" columns |

All three share Song 2016 Equation 1 with the additive residual error of
Equation 2:

$$
\Delta\Delta \mathrm{QTc}_{ij} = \theta_1 (1 + \omega_1)
  + \theta_2\,\Delta\Delta \mathrm{RR}_{ij} (1 + \omega_2)
  + \theta_3\,\mathrm{OMconc}_{ij} (1 + \omega_3) + \sigma_i
$$

The random effects are proportional to each coefficient. In the model files the
three coefficients are `e0` (intercept), `e_rr_delta_e0` (DeltaDeltaRR) and
`slope` (olmesartan concentration). Their random effects are `etae0`,
`etae_rr_delta_e0` and `etaslope`, and the residual is `addSd`.

The "QTc" columns of Table 2 are the uncorrected QT interval. Figure 1 and
Supplemental Figure S1 label the same endpoint "DeltaDeltaQT". Its DeltaDeltaRR
coefficient, 0.128 ms/ms, matches the slope of raw QT on RR in Figure 1
(0.124 ms/ms), and Song 2016 states it is 380-fold and 20-fold larger than the
QTcF and QTcP coefficients. The model's own DeltaDeltaRR term does the heart-rate
correction. The file keeps the paper's name and the generic `QTc` output.

Covariates in the model files:

* `CP_OLMESARTAN_NGML` -- olmesartan plasma concentration at the ECG time
  (ng/mL).
* `RR_DELTA` -- baseline-adjusted, time-matched placebo-adjusted RR interval
  (ms). Set it to 0 for the heart-rate-neutral prediction.

These are PD-only models: concentrations are inputs. The library's olmesartan
population PK model, `Song_2013_olmesartan`, is used below to drive them over
the study's ECG schedule.

# Population

The study randomised 56 healthy subjects (28 men, 28 women), and 51
completed. The cardiodynamic and pharmacokinetic analysis sets each had 55
subjects (Song 2016 Methods). Mean age was 31.9 years (range 19-45) and mean
body mass index 26.2 kg/m^2 (range 19.1-30.6). The companion report (Mendell
2016 Table 1) gives 91.1% White, 7.1% Black or African American, 1.8% American
Indian or Alaska Native and 85.7% Hispanic or Latino. Triplicate ECGs were
extracted from Holter recordings at the PK sampling times, predose and at 0.5,
1, 1.5, 2, 2.5, 3, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12 and 24 h postdose. Only the two olmesartan
treatments entered the concentration-QTc model, which was fitted with NONMEM
7.1.0 (FOCE with interaction).

# Source trace

| Element | QTc model | QTcF model | QTcP model | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Model structure | Equations 1 and 2 | same | same | Results, "Exposure-Response Analysis" |
| `e0` (intercept, ms) | -0.15 | -0.129 | -0.156 | Table 2 |
| `slope` (ms per ng/mL) | 0.000807 | 0.000816 | 0.000800 | Table 2; Results text |
| `e_rr_delta_e0` (ms per ms) | 0.128 | 0.000336 | 0.00646 | Table 2 |
| `etae0` (printed "omega2 Intercept") | 4.81 -> 23.1361 | -5.73 -> 32.8329 | 4.63 -> 21.4369 | Table 2; see Assumptions |
| `etaslope` (printed "omega2 beta OMconc") | 3.37 -> 11.3569 | 3.27 -> 10.6929 | 3.31 -> 10.9561 | Table 2; see Assumptions |
| `etae_rr_delta_e0` (printed "omega2 ddRR") | -0.315 -> 0.099225 | -108 -> 11664 | -5.58 -> 31.1364 | Table 2; see Assumptions |
| `addSd` (printed "sigma2", ms) | 4.03 | 3.99 | 3.99 | Table 2; see Assumptions |
| QTcP correction coefficient | -- | -- | 3.265 | Methods, "Evaluation of Population QT Correction Coefficients" |
| Validation targets | DeltaDeltaQTc 1.815 ms at 2440 ng/mL | slope CV 0.99% across endpoints | RR coefficient ratios 380 and 20 | Results |

# Models

```{r models}
mod <- list(
  QTc = readModelDb("Song_2016_olmesartan_QTc"),
  QTcF = readModelDb("Song_2016_olmesartan_QTcF"),
  QTcP = readModelDb("Song_2016_olmesartan_QTcP")
)
mod_typ <- lapply(mod, rxode2::zeroRe)

# Table 2 values, used below for the identity and published-number checks
tab2 <- data.frame(
  endpoint = c("QTc", "QTcF", "QTcP"),
  e0 = c(-0.15, -0.129, -0.156),
  slope = c(0.000807, 0.000816, 0.000800),
  rr = c(0.128, 0.000336, 0.00646),
  w_e0 = c(4.81, -5.73, 4.63),
  w_slope = c(3.37, 3.27, 3.31),
  w_rr = c(-0.315, -108, -5.58),
  sigma = c(4.03, 3.99, 3.99)
)

# PD-only event table: no dosing records and no ODE states; both covariates are
# columns. The models are algebraic, so typical-value rows can share one id.
pd_events <- function(conc, rr_delta = 0) {
  n <- max(length(conc), length(rr_delta))
  data.frame(
    id = 1L, time = seq_len(n), evid = 0L, amt = 0,
    CP_OLMESARTAN_NGML = rep_len(conc, n),
    RR_DELTA = rep_len(rr_delta, n)
  )
}

solve_typ <- function(endpoint, ev) {
  as.data.frame(rxode2::rxSolve(mod_typ[[endpoint]], events = ev))[[endpoint]]
}
```

# Structural checks

With the random effects at zero, each model must equal
`e0 + e_rr_delta_e0 * RR_DELTA + slope * C` for any concentration and
DeltaDeltaRR. These are identities of the encoding and are asserted at machine
precision.

```{r structural}
grid <- expand.grid(conc = c(0, 500, 2440, 4500), rr = c(-300, 0, 150))
for (k in seq_len(nrow(tab2))) {
  ep <- tab2$endpoint[k]
  got <- solve_typ(ep, pd_events(grid$conc, grid$rr))
  want <- tab2$e0[k] + tab2$rr[k] * grid$rr + tab2$slope[k] * grid$conc
  stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(got, want, tolerance = 1e-12)))
}
```

# Published numbers

Song 2016 reports three numbers derived from the final models:

* the predicted mean DeltaDeltaQTc of 1.815 ms at 2440 ng/mL. That
  concentration is the mean Cmax after 160 mg in Mendell 2016, which Song 2016
  calls the highest observed concentration. The prediction has DeltaDeltaRR at
  0 and uses the "QTc" model;
* a coefficient of variation of 0.99% among the three concentration slopes;
* DeltaDeltaRR coefficients for QTc that are 380-fold and 20-fold those for QTcF
  and QTcP.

```{r published}
pred_2440 <- solve_typ("QTc", pd_events(2440))
slope_cv <- 100 * sd(tab2$slope) / mean(tab2$slope)
rr_ratio <- tab2$rr[1] / tab2$rr[2:3]

stopifnot(
  # 1.815 is printed to 0.001 ms; the 6-significant-figure slope reproduces it
  # to within that rounding of the slope (2440 * 0.0000005 = 0.0012 ms).
  abs(pred_2440 - 1.815) < 0.005,
  abs(slope_cv - 0.99) < 0.005,
  abs(rr_ratio[1] - 380) / 380 < 0.01,
  abs(rr_ratio[2] - 20) / 20 < 0.02
)

data.frame(
  Quantity = c(
    "DeltaDeltaQTc at 2440 ng/mL (ms)",
    "CV of the three olmesartan slopes (%)",
    "RR coefficient ratio QTc / QTcF",
    "RR coefficient ratio QTc / QTcP"
  ),
  Published = c(1.815, 0.99, 380, 20),
  Model = c(pred_2440, slope_cv, rr_ratio)
) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3, caption = "Numbers stated in the Results of Song 2016.")
```

The 90% confidence interval that Song 2016 gives at 2440 ng/mL (0.024 to 3.606
ms) depends on the sampling covariance of the intercept and slope, which is not
reported, so it is not reproduced.

Figure 1 (panels 4-6) also prints ordinary least-squares slopes of each
DeltaDelta endpoint on DeltaDeltaRR, with no concentration term and no random
effects. These are not model parameters, but they are of the same size as the
fitted RR coefficients: 0.125 versus 0.128 ms/ms for QT, -0.005 versus 0.0003
for QTcF and 0.006 versus 0.0065 for QTcP.

```{r fig-cr, fig.cap = "Typical DeltaDelta prediction against olmesartan concentration at DeltaDeltaRR = 0, for the three endpoints. Points mark the mean Cmax after 40 mg (863 ng/mL) and 160 mg (2440 ng/mL) from Mendell 2016; the dotted line is the 10 ms threshold of ICH E14."}
conc_grid <- seq(0, 4500, by = 50)
curve_df <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(tab2$endpoint, function(ep) {
  data.frame(endpoint = ep, conc = conc_grid, value = solve_typ(ep, pd_events(conc_grid)))
}))
cmax_df <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(tab2$endpoint, function(ep) {
  data.frame(endpoint = ep, conc = c(863.3, 2440), value = solve_typ(ep, pd_events(c(863.3, 2440))))
}))
ggplot(curve_df, aes(conc, value, colour = endpoint)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point(data = cmax_df, size = 2) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 10, linetype = "dotted") +
  labs(
    x = "Olmesartan concentration (ng/mL)",
    y = "Typical DeltaDelta interval (ms)",
    colour = "Endpoint"
  ) +
  theme_bw()
```

# Scale of the random effects

Table 2 heads the random-effect rows "omega2", but four of the nine printed
values are negative (-5.73, -0.315, -108 and -5.58). A variance cannot be
negative. So the printed values are the standard deviations of the proportional
random effects, each a NONMEM THETA multiplying a unit-variance ETA, whose sign
does not matter. The model files use the square of each printed value as the
eta variance.

A second check confirms this reading. QT, QTcF and QTcP for one subject differ
only by a correction applied to that subject's QT. A subject's own sensitivity
to DeltaDeltaRR should therefore shift between endpoints by about the same
amount for everyone, and its spread across subjects should not depend on the
endpoint. The absolute between-subject SD of each coefficient is
`|theta| * SD(eta)`. Under the SD reading it is nearly constant across the
three endpoints for all three coefficients. Under the variance reading,
`|theta| * sqrt(omega2)`, the DeltaDeltaRR coefficient's SD differs 20-fold
between endpoints.

```{r re-scale}
sd_reading <- with(tab2, cbind(
  intercept = abs(e0 * w_e0), slope = abs(slope * w_slope), rr = abs(rr * w_rr)
))
var_reading <- with(tab2, cbind(
  intercept = abs(e0) * sqrt(abs(w_e0)), slope = abs(slope) * sqrt(abs(w_slope)),
  rr = abs(rr) * sqrt(abs(w_rr))
))
spread <- function(m) apply(m, 2, function(x) max(x) / min(x))

# The model files carry exactly the SD reading.
for (k in seq_len(nrow(tab2))) {
  om <- diag(rxode2::rxode2(mod[[tab2$endpoint[k]]])$omega)
  stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(
    unname(om[c("etae0", "etaslope", "etae_rr_delta_e0")]),
    c(tab2$w_e0[k], tab2$w_slope[k], tab2$w_rr[k])^2
  )))
}

stopifnot(
  all(spread(sd_reading) < 1.15),
  spread(var_reading)[["rr"]] > 10
)

rbind(
  data.frame(reading = "SD (used)", endpoint = tab2$endpoint, sd_reading),
  data.frame(reading = "variance", endpoint = tab2$endpoint, var_reading)
) |>
  dplyr::rename(
    "Reading of 'omega2'" = reading,
    "Endpoint" = endpoint,
    "Intercept SD (ms)" = intercept,
    "Slope SD (ms per ng/mL)" = slope,
    "DeltaDeltaRR coefficient SD (ms/ms)" = rr
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(
    digits = 5,
    caption = "Absolute between-subject SD of each coefficient under the two readings of Table 2."
  )
```

The residual row ("sigma2") is read the same way, as an SD of 4.03 or 3.99 ms
(see Assumptions).

# Simulation of the thorough QTc study

## Olmesartan concentrations

The models need a concentration at each ECG time. The library's olmesartan
population PK model `Song_2013_olmesartan` provides one. It was developed in
hypertensive patients and healthy volunteers at 20-40 mg, so it is not a model
of this study. Its covariates are set to the reference values (creatinine
clearance 111 mL/min, weight 91.5 kg), and the dose is the nominal olmesartan
medoxomil dose. As a check on how well it describes this study, its
typical-value profiles are compared below, with PKNCA, against the mean NCA
results of Mendell 2016.

```{r pk-typical}
pk_mod <- readModelDb("Song_2013_olmesartan")
pk_typ <- rxode2::zeroRe(pk_mod)

pk_grid <- sort(unique(c(seq(0, 12, by = 0.25), seq(13, 72, by = 1))))
pk_events <- function(ids, doses, times) {
  dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(seq_along(ids), function(k) {
    rbind(
      data.frame(id = ids[k], time = 0, evid = 1L, amt = doses[k], cmt = "depot"),
      data.frame(id = ids[k], time = times, evid = 0L, amt = 0, cmt = "central")
    )
  }))
}
ev_pk_typ <- pk_events(1:2, c(40, 160), pk_grid)
ev_pk_typ$CRCL <- 111
ev_pk_typ$WT <- 91.5

pk_typ_sim <- as.data.frame(rxode2::rxSolve(pk_typ, events = ev_pk_typ)) |>
  dplyr::mutate(treatment = ifelse(id == 1, "40 mg", "160 mg"))

conc_pk <- pk_typ_sim |>
  dplyr::filter(!is.na(Cc)) |>
  dplyr::select(id, treatment, time, Cc)
dose_pk <- data.frame(id = 1:2, treatment = c("40 mg", "160 mg"), time = 0, amt = c(40, 160))

nca_res <- PKNCA::pk.nca(PKNCA::PKNCAdata(
  PKNCA::PKNCAconc(conc_pk, Cc ~ time | treatment + id),
  PKNCA::PKNCAdose(dose_pk, amt ~ time | treatment + id),
  intervals = data.frame(start = 0, end = Inf, cmax = TRUE, aucinf.obs = TRUE, half.life = TRUE)
))

mendell <- data.frame(
  treatment = c("40 mg", "160 mg"),
  cmax = c(863.3, 2440),
  aucinf.obs = c(5544, 18243),
  half.life = c(10.2, 12.0)
)
cmp <- nlmixr2lib::ncaComparisonTable(
  simulated = nca_res,
  reference = mendell,
  by = "treatment",
  units = c(cmax = "ng/mL", aucinf.obs = "ng*h/mL", half.life = "h"),
  tolerance_pct = 20
)
knitr::kable(cmp, caption = "Typical-value NCA of Song_2013_olmesartan against the mean NCA of the thorough QTc study (Mendell 2016).")
```

```{r pk-footnote, echo = FALSE, results = "asis"}
if (!is.null(attr(cmp, "footnote"))) cat(attr(cmp, "footnote"), "\n")
```

At 40 mg the typical Cmax and AUC are within 15% of the study means. The
typical terminal half-life (16.3 h) is longer than the study's 10.2-12.0 h,
which come from single-dose NCA over 72 h in healthy adults. The half-life does
not enter the concentration-QTc models, which use only the concentration at
each ECG time. At 160 mg the linear PK model also overpredicts Cmax and AUC, because
olmesartan exposure rises less than in proportion to dose. Mendell 2016 reports a 3.3-fold rise in AUC
and a 2.8-fold rise in Cmax for the 4-fold rise in dose. The QTc predictions
below at 160 mg are therefore made at higher concentrations than the study
achieved. They are conservative, and they do not test the concentration-QTc
models.

## Virtual crossover cohort

Each of 200 virtual subjects receives both doses in separate periods. One
subject's random effects on the QTc coefficients are shared across periods.
Olmesartan concentrations come from a stochastic solve of `Song_2013_olmesartan`
at the 12 postdose ECG times, with between-subject variability. DeltaDeltaRR is
not modelled by the paper. Each ECG draws it independently from a normal
distribution with mean 0 and SD 100 ms, a spread read from the -350 to +300 ms
range of Figure 1 (panels 4-6). The three endpoint models are solved on the
same records.

```{r cohort}
set.seed(20160101)
n_sub <- 200
ecg_times <- c(0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 2.5, 3, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 24)

# PK: one id per subject-period, so each period is a separate single dose
pk_ids <- data.frame(
  pk_id = seq_len(2 * n_sub),
  subject = rep(seq_len(n_sub), times = 2),
  treatment = rep(c("40 mg", "160 mg"), each = n_sub),
  dose = rep(c(40, 160), each = n_sub)
)
ev_pk <- pk_events(pk_ids$pk_id, pk_ids$dose, ecg_times)
ev_pk$CRCL <- 111
ev_pk$WT <- 91.5
pk_sim <- as.data.frame(rxode2::rxSolve(pk_mod, events = ev_pk)) |>
  dplyr::select(pk_id = id, tad = time, Cc) |>
  dplyr::left_join(pk_ids, by = "pk_id")

# QTc records: one id per subject, the 160 mg period offset by 100 h so the
# two periods share the subject's random effects without overlapping in time.
qt_records <- pk_sim |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    id = subject,
    time = tad + ifelse(treatment == "160 mg", 100, 0),
    evid = 0L, amt = 0,
    CP_OLMESARTAN_NGML = Cc,
    RR_DELTA = rnorm(dplyr::n(), 0, 100)
  ) |>
  dplyr::arrange(id, time)

sims <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(tab2$endpoint, function(ep) {
  ev <- qt_records |> dplyr::select(id, time, evid, amt, CP_OLMESARTAN_NGML, RR_DELTA)
  s <- as.data.frame(rxode2::rxSolve(mod[[ep]], events = ev))
  data.frame(
    endpoint = ep, id = s$id, time = s$time,
    conc = s$CP_OLMESARTAN_NGML, rr_delta = s$RR_DELTA,
    ipred = s[[ep]], sim = s$sim
  )
})) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    treatment = ifelse(time > 50, "160 mg", "40 mg"),
    tad = ifelse(time > 50, time - 100, time)
  )
```

```{r fig-time, fig.cap = "Simulated DeltaDeltaQTcF over time after single doses of 40 mg and 160 mg olmesartan medoxomil (median and 5th-95th percentiles of the individual predictions, 200 subjects, DeltaDeltaRR drawn as described). The dotted line is the 10 ms threshold."}
sims |>
  dplyr::filter(endpoint == "QTcF") |>
  dplyr::group_by(treatment, tad) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    med = median(ipred), lo = quantile(ipred, 0.05), hi = quantile(ipred, 0.95),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(tad, med, colour = treatment, fill = treatment)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), alpha = 0.2, colour = NA) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 10, linetype = "dotted") +
  labs(x = "Time after dose (h)", y = "DeltaDeltaQTcF individual prediction (ms)",
       colour = "Dose", fill = "Dose") +
  theme_bw()
```

```{r fig-gof, fig.cap = "Simulated observations against individual predictions for the three endpoints. Compare with the left column of Supplemental Figure S1 of Song 2016."}
ggplot(sims, aes(ipred, sim)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.15, size = 0.6) +
  geom_abline(colour = "red") +
  facet_wrap(~endpoint, scales = "free") +
  labs(x = "Individual prediction (ms)", y = "Simulated observation (ms)") +
  theme_bw()
```

## Checks on the stochastic simulation

Three properties are checked on the robust centre and spread of the cohort.

* The residual (simulated value minus individual prediction) has the `addSd`
  SD. With 4800 records per endpoint the standard error of an SD estimate is
  about 1%, so a 10% band is wide against sampling noise.
* The random effects have zero mean, so the median of the individual predictions
  minus the typical prediction at each record's own covariates is near 0.
* The spread of the individual predictions for QTcF and QTcP comes mainly from
  the between-subject variation in the DeltaDeltaRR and concentration
  coefficients. In Supplemental Figure S1 the individual predictions of
  DeltaDeltaQTcF and DeltaDeltaQTcP span about -20 to +19 ms (a full range of
  about 39 ms) around population predictions within a few ms of 0. The same
  records are also evaluated with random effects drawn under the variance
  reading. Under the SD reading the 1st-99th percentile width of the individual
  predictions is about 30 ms, consistent with the figure's full range. Under the
  variance reading it is less than half the figure's range. The check requires
  the SD-reading width to lie between 20 and 50 ms and to be at least 1.5 times
  the variance-reading width. The uncorrected QT endpoint is not included,
  because its spread comes from the fixed 0.128 ms/ms DeltaDeltaRR coefficient
  under either reading.

```{r stochastic-checks}
typ <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(tab2$endpoint, function(ep) {
  ev <- qt_records |> dplyr::mutate(id = 1L, time = seq_len(dplyr::n()))
  data.frame(endpoint = ep, typ = solve_typ(ep, ev |> dplyr::select(id, time, evid, amt, CP_OLMESARTAN_NGML, RR_DELTA)))
}))
sims$typ <- typ$typ

# Individual predictions on the same records with the per-subject random
# effects drawn under the variance reading (SD of eta = sqrt(|printed value|)).
var_w98_all <- vapply(seq_len(nrow(tab2)), function(k) {
  eta <- data.frame(
    id = seq_len(n_sub),
    e_e0 = rnorm(n_sub, 0, sqrt(abs(tab2$w_e0[k]))),
    e_slope = rnorm(n_sub, 0, sqrt(abs(tab2$w_slope[k]))),
    e_rr = rnorm(n_sub, 0, sqrt(abs(tab2$w_rr[k])))
  )
  x <- dplyr::left_join(qt_records, eta, by = "id") |>
    dplyr::mutate(ipred = tab2$e0[k] * (1 + e_e0) + tab2$rr[k] * (1 + e_rr) * RR_DELTA +
      tab2$slope[k] * (1 + e_slope) * CP_OLMESARTAN_NGML)
  unname(diff(quantile(x$ipred, c(0.01, 0.99))))
}, numeric(1))
names(var_w98_all) <- tab2$endpoint

sim_check <- sims |>
  dplyr::group_by(endpoint) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    resid_sd = sd(sim - ipred),
    med_dev = median(ipred - typ),
    ipred_w98 = unname(diff(quantile(ipred, c(0.01, 0.99)))),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  dplyr::left_join(tab2 |> dplyr::select(endpoint, sigma), by = "endpoint") |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    resid_pct = 100 * (resid_sd - sigma) / sigma,
    var_w98 = unname(var_w98_all[endpoint])
  )

stopifnot(
  all(abs(sim_check$resid_pct) < 10),
  all(abs(sim_check$med_dev) < 1),
  all(dplyr::between(sim_check$ipred_w98[sim_check$endpoint %in% c("QTcF", "QTcP")], 20, 50)),
  all(with(sim_check[sim_check$endpoint %in% c("QTcF", "QTcP"), ], ipred_w98 / var_w98) > 1.5)
)

sim_check |>
  dplyr::select(endpoint, sigma, resid_sd, resid_pct, med_dev, ipred_w98, var_w98) |>
  dplyr::rename(
    "Endpoint" = endpoint,
    "Model residual SD (ms)" = sigma,
    "Simulated residual SD (ms)" = resid_sd,
    "% diff" = resid_pct,
    "Median individual minus typical (ms)" = med_dev,
    "Width of 1st-99th percentile of individual predictions (ms)" = ipred_w98,
    "Same, variance reading (ms)" = var_w98
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 2, caption = "Summary of the simulated cohort.")
```

# Assumptions and deviations

* **Random-effect scale.** Table 2 heads the random-effect rows "omega2", but
  four printed values are negative, which a variance cannot be. The models read
  each printed value as the SD of a proportional random effect, the coefficient
  of a unit-variance eta (eta variance = printed value squared). Two checks
  support this reading. The absolute between-subject SD of each coefficient is
  consistent across the three endpoints (Scale of the random effects, above).
  The spread of the individual predictions in Supplemental Figure S1 also
  matches it (Checks on the stochastic simulation). The variance reading fails
  both checks.
* **Residual scale.** Table 2 heads the residual row "sigma2". It is read as an
  SD (4.03 and 3.99 ms), for consistency with the "omega2" rows. Supplemental
  Figure S1 supports this: the observed values scatter about the individual
  predictions with a band of roughly +/-10 ms and many points 15-20 ms away. An
  SD of 2.0 ms (the square root, if "sigma2" were a variance) would put those
  points 8 or more SDs out.
* **Standard error printed as "2.6.1".** The standard error of the QTcF
  DeltaDeltaRR random effect (-108) is printed as "2.6.1". It is not used by
  the model.
* **"QTc" is uncorrected QT.** Table 2's footnote expands "QTc" as "corrected QT
  interval", while Figure 1 and Supplemental Figure S1 label the same endpoint
  "DeltaDeltaQT" (uncorrected). The DeltaDeltaRR coefficient of 0.128 ms/ms
  matches the raw QT-RR slope. The file `Song_2016_olmesartan_QTc` is therefore
  the uncorrected QT model, with heart rate corrected by its own DeltaDeltaRR
  term.
* **"Highest observed" concentration.** Song 2016 calls 2440 ng/mL the highest
  observed concentration after 160 mg. The companion study report gives it as
  the mean Cmax after 160 mg (2440 +/- 678 ng/mL). This does not change the
  1.815 ms check, which is a prediction at a stated concentration.
* **Not packaged.** The intermediate models of Table 1 (intercept only, with
  DeltaDeltaRR, without the intercept) are not packaged. The paper presents
  them as model-building steps toward the final model.
* **Simulation inputs.** The PK driver (`Song_2013_olmesartan`, typical
  covariates, nominal medoxomil dose, linear in dose) and the DeltaDeltaRR
  distribution (normal, SD 100 ms, independent between ECGs and of
  concentration) are assumptions of this vignette. They do not affect the
  model files.
